title: Global Physical Climatology
text:
Preface
This book covers global physical climatology and machine learning approaches including PINNs and Neural Operators.

title: Vector Calculus
text: Builds the differential operator vocabulary used throughout the book. Covers gradient (scalar and vector fields), the Jacobian, directional derivative, divergence, curl, and the Laplacian. Derives all operators in spherical coordinates via scale factors, and identifies the Laplace-Beltrami operator on \(S^2\). Covers line, surface, and volume integrals, and the integral theorems: Green’s, Stokes’, and the Divergence theorem.

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.1 Gradient
Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) be a scalar field and \(\mathbf{F} : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) a vector field with components \(\mathbf{F} = (F_x, F_y, F_z)\).
Definition (scalar field). The gradient of \(f : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) is the vector field
\[\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial y},\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right).\]
Intuition. \(\nabla f(\mathbf{p})\) points in the direction of steepest increase of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{p}\). Its magnitude is the rate of change in that direction. Level sets of \(f\) are everywhere perpendicular to \(\nabla f\).
Example. Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2\). Then \(\nabla f = (2x, 2y)\). At \(\mathbf{p} = (1, 1)\): \(\nabla f = (2, 2)\), pointing radially outward with magnitude \(2\sqrt{2}\).
Definition (vector field). The gradient of \(\mathbf{F} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is the \(m \times n\) tensor of partial derivatives
\[(\nabla \mathbf{F})_{ij} = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}.\]
This is a second-order tensor (matrix). It maps a direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) to the directional derivative \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} \mathbf{F} = (\nabla \mathbf{F})\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}\), generalizing the scalar case.
Example. Let \(\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (x^2 + y,\; xy)\). Then
\[\nabla \mathbf{F} = \begin{pmatrix} 2x & 1 \\ y & x \end{pmatrix}.\]
At \(\mathbf{p} = (1, 2)\): \(\nabla \mathbf{F} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.7 (scalar gradient and directional derivative); tensor gradient of vector fields is treated more fully in advanced calculus texts.

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.2 Jacobian
Definition. For \(\mathbf{F} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\), the Jacobian matrix \(J_\mathbf{F}\) is identical to \(\nabla \mathbf{F}\):
\[J_\mathbf{F} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial F_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}.\]
The Jacobian is the best linear approximation to \(\mathbf{F}\) at a point: \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{h}) \approx \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{p}) + J_\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{p})\,\mathbf{h}\).
Jacobian determinant. For square \(\mathbf{F} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\), \(\det(J_\mathbf{F})\) measures local volume scaling under \(\mathbf{F}\). It appears in the change-of-variables formula:
\[\int_{\mathbf{F}(V)} g(\mathbf{y})\, d\mathbf{y} = \int_V g(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}))\,|\det J_\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x})|\, d\mathbf{x}.\]
Example. The map to spherical coordinates \(\mathbf{F}(r, \theta, \phi) = (r\sin\theta\cos\phi,\; r\sin\theta\sin\phi,\; r\cos\theta)\) has
\[\det(J_\mathbf{F}) = r^2 \sin\theta,\]
giving the volume element \(dV = r^2\sin\theta\, dr\, d\theta\, d\phi\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.6 (calculus review, change of variables) and Sec. 10.7 (Jacobian in the context of triple integrals).

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.3 Directional Derivative
Definition. The directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{p}\) along unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) is
\[D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{p}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}.\]
This is the rate of change of \(f\) along \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\). The gradient is the unique direction that maximizes \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f\), with maximum value \(|\nabla f(\mathbf{p})|\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.7.

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.4 Divergence
Definition. The divergence of \(\mathbf{F}\) is the scalar field
\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}.\]
Intuition. \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{p})\) measures the net outward flux of \(\mathbf{F}\) per unit volume at \(\mathbf{p}\). Positive divergence indicates a local source; negative indicates a sink; zero indicates incompressibility.
Example. Let \(\mathbf{F}(x, y, z) = (x, y, z)\) (radial expansion). Then
\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.\]
Uniform positive divergence everywhere: every point is a source.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.8.

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.5 Curl
Definition. The curl of \(\mathbf{F}\) is the vector field
\[\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{x}} & \hat{\mathbf{y}} & \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\ F_x & F_y & F_z \end{vmatrix} = \left(\frac{\partial F_z}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial z},\; \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial x},\; \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}\right).\]
Intuition. \(\nabla \times \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{p})\) measures the infinitesimal rotation of \(\mathbf{F}\) at \(\mathbf{p}\). Its direction is the axis of rotation (right-hand rule); its magnitude is twice the angular velocity. A field with \(\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}\) everywhere is called irrotational.
Example. Let \(\mathbf{F}(x, y, z) = (-y, x, 0)\), solid-body rotation in the \(xy\)-plane. Then
\[\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \left(0 - 0,\; 0 - 0,\; 1 - (-1)\right) = (0, 0, 2).\]
The rotation axis is \(+\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) with angular velocity \(1\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.9.

title: 1  Differential Operators
text:
1.6 Laplacian
Definition. The Laplacian of \(f\) is
\[\nabla^2 f = \nabla \cdot (\nabla f) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}.\]
For a vector field, the Laplacian acts component-wise: \(\nabla^2 \mathbf{F} = (\nabla^2 F_x, \nabla^2 F_y, \nabla^2 F_z)\).
Intuition. \(\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{p})\) is proportional to the difference between \(f(\mathbf{p})\) and the average of \(f\) over an infinitesimal sphere centered at \(\mathbf{p}\). It governs diffusion, electrostatics, and fluid flow. The equation \(\nabla^2 f = 0\) (Laplace equation) characterizes fields with no local sources or sinks.
Example. Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\). Then \(\nabla^2 f = 2 - 2 = 0\): this function satisfies the Laplace equation.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.8 (Laplacian as div of grad); Evans (2010), Ch. 2 (Laplace equation and its properties).




Evans, Lawrence C. 2010. Partial Differential Equations. 2nd ed. American Mathematical Society.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 2  Integrals
text:
2.1 Line Integral
Let \(C\) be a smooth curve parametrized by \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), \(t \in [a, b]\).
Scalar form:
\[\int_C f \, ds = \int_a^b f(\mathbf{r}(t))\, |\mathbf{r}'(t)|\, dt.\]
Vector form (work):
\[\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)\, dt.\]
Example. Let \(\mathbf{F} = (y, 0)\) and \(C\) the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\) parametrized as \(\mathbf{r}(t) = (t, t)\), \(t \in [0,1]\). Then \(\mathbf{r}'(t) = (1,1)\) and \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) = (t, 0)\), so
\[\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_0^1 t \, dt = \frac{1}{2}.\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.1.

title: 2  Integrals
text:
2.2 Surface Integral
Let \(S\) be an oriented surface with unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) and area element \(dS\).
Scalar form:
\[\iint_S f \, dS.\]
Flux form:
\[\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \, dS.\]
Example. Let \(\mathbf{F} = (0, 0, 1)\) and \(S\) the unit disk in the \(xy\)-plane with \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (0, 0, 1)\). Then \(\mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 1\) everywhere, so the flux is
\[\iint_S dS = \pi.\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Secs. 10.5-10.6.

title: 2  Integrals
text:
2.3 Volume Integral
\[\iiint_V f \, dV = \iiint_V f(x, y, z)\, dx\, dy\, dz.\]
Example. \(f(x,y,z) = z\) over the unit cube \([0,1]^3\):
\[\iiint_{[0,1]^3} z \, dV = \int_0^1 z \, dz = \frac{1}{2}.\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.7.




Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 3  Change of Variables
text:
3.1 General Theorem
When an integral is computed over a domain that is not naturally aligned with Cartesian coordinates, a change of variables can simplify the computation. The Jacobian determinant (defined in the operators section) is the key quantity that accounts for the local volume distortion introduced by the coordinate map.
Let \(\mathbf{G} : U \to V\) be a smooth, invertible map between open sets \(U, V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), with \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{u})\). Then
\[\int_V f(\mathbf{x})\, d\mathbf{x} = \int_U f(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{u}))\, |\det J_\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{u})|\, d\mathbf{u},\]
where \(J_\mathbf{G}\) is the Jacobian of \(\mathbf{G}\). The factor \(|\det J_\mathbf{G}|\) converts the volume element \(d\mathbf{u}\) in the new coordinates to the corresponding volume element \(d\mathbf{x}\) in the original coordinates.
1D case. For \(x = g(u)\) with \(g\) monotone:
\[\int_a^b f(x)\, dx = \int_{g^{-1}(a)}^{g^{-1}(b)} f(g(u))\, |g'(u)|\, du.\]
The factor \(|g'(u)|\) is the 1D Jacobian determinant.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.7 (change of variables in double and triple integrals).

title: 3  Change of Variables
text:
3.2 Polar Coordinates in 2D
The polar coordinate map is \(\mathbf{G}(r, \theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\), so
\[J_\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det J_\mathbf{G} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r.\]
The area element transforms as \(dA = r\, dr\, d\theta\).
Example. Compute \(I = \iint_D e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}\, dA\) over the unit disk \(D = \{x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}\).
In polar coordinates \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) and the disk becomes \(r \in [0,1]\), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\):
\[I = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 e^{-r^2}\, r\, dr\, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^1 r e^{-r^2}\, dr = 2\pi \left[-\tfrac{1}{2}e^{-r^2}\right]_0^1 = \pi(1 - e^{-1}).\]

title: 3  Change of Variables
text:
3.3 Spherical Coordinates in 3D
As derived in the spherical coordinates section, the Jacobian determinant of the spherical coordinate map \((r, \theta, \phi) \mapsto (x, y, z)\) is \(\det J = r^2\sin\theta\), giving the volume element
\[dV = r^2\sin\theta\, dr\, d\theta\, d\phi.\]
Example 1: Volume of a ball. Let \(B_R = \{|\mathbf{x}| \leq R\}\). Then
\[\text{Vol}(B_R) = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\int_0^R r^2\sin\theta\, dr\, d\theta\, d\phi = 2\pi \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{R^3}{3} = \frac{4\pi R^3}{3}.\]
Example 2: Surface area of the unit sphere. Setting \(r = 1\) constant, the area element on \(S^2\) is \(d\Omega = \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi\):
\[\text{Area}(S^2) = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi} \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi = 2\pi \cdot 2 = 4\pi.\]
Example 3: Gaussian integral in 3D. Compute \(I = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^3} e^{-r^2}\, dV\):
\[I = \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^{\pi} \sin\theta\, d\theta \int_0^{\infty} e^{-r^2} r^2\, dr = 4\pi \int_0^{\infty} r^2 e^{-r^2}\, dr.\]
Using \(\int_0^\infty r^2 e^{-r^2}\, dr = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4}\):
\[I = 4\pi \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4} = \pi^{3/2}.\]
This equals \(\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2}\, dx\right)^3 = (\sqrt{\pi})^3\), confirming consistency with the 1D Gaussian integral.




Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 4  Integral Theorems
text:
4.1 Green’s Theorem
Let \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) be a bounded region with piecewise smooth positively oriented boundary \(\partial D\). For \(P, Q \in C^1(\bar{D})\):
\[\oint_{\partial D} \bigl(P\, dx + Q\, dy\bigr) = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) dA.\]
With \(\mathbf{F} = (P, Q, 0)\), the right side is \(\iint_D (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} \, dA\). Green’s theorem is the two-dimensional special case of Stokes’ theorem.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.4.

title: 4  Integral Theorems
text:
4.2 Stokes’ Theorem
Let \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) be an oriented surface with piecewise smooth boundary \(\partial S\), oriented by the right-hand rule relative to \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\). For \(\mathbf{F} \in C^1(S)\):
\[\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}.\]
The circulation of \(\mathbf{F}\) around the boundary equals the flux of its curl through the surface.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.9.

title: 4  Integral Theorems
text:
4.3 Divergence Theorem
Let \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) be a bounded region with piecewise smooth outward-oriented boundary \(\partial V\). For \(\mathbf{F} \in C^1(\bar{V})\):
\[\iint_{\partial V} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} \, dV.\]
The total outward flux through the boundary equals the integral of the divergence over the volume. This theorem is central to the derivation of Green’s identities, which underpin Green’s functions in the PDEs chapter.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.7; Evans (2010), Appendix C.2 (Green’s identities as a direct corollary).




Evans, Lawrence C. 2010. Partial Differential Equations. 2nd ed. American Mathematical Society.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
text:
5.1 Coordinate System
Spherical coordinates \((r, \theta, \phi)\) relate to Cartesian coordinates by
\[x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi, \quad y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi, \quad z = r\cos\theta,\]
where \(r \geq 0\) is the radial distance, \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) is the polar angle (colatitude, from the north pole), and \(\phi \in [0, 2\pi)\) is the azimuthal angle (longitude). The orthonormal basis \((\hat{r}, \hat{\theta}, \hat{\phi})\) points in the directions of increasing \(r\), \(\theta\), \(\phi\) respectively, and rotates with position.

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
text:
5.2 Scale Factors
For an orthogonal curvilinear coordinate system \((q_1, q_2, q_3)\), the scale factors are
\[h_i = \left|\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial q_i}\right|,\]
converting coordinate differentials to physical arc lengths: \(ds_i = h_i\, dq_i\). The volume element is \(dV = h_1 h_2 h_3\, dq_1\, dq_2\, dq_3\).
For spherical coordinates, computing \(\partial \mathbf{r}/\partial r\), \(\partial \mathbf{r}/\partial \theta\), \(\partial \mathbf{r}/\partial \phi\) and taking magnitudes gives
\[h_r = 1, \qquad h_\theta = r, \qquad h_\phi = r\sin\theta,\]
and hence \(dV = r^2\sin\theta\, dr\, d\theta\, d\phi\), consistent with the Jacobian determinant from the operators section.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 10.7 (spherical volume element in the context of triple integrals).

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
section: 5.3 General Operator Formulas for Orthogonal Curvilinear Coordinates
text:
5.3 General Operator Formulas for Orthogonal Curvilinear Coordinates
For coordinates \((q_1, q_2, q_3)\) with scale factors \((h_1, h_2, h_3)\) and vector field \(\mathbf{F} = F_1\hat{e}_1 + F_2\hat{e}_2 + F_3\hat{e}_3\):
Gradient: \[\nabla f = \frac{1}{h_1}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_1}\hat{e}_1 + \frac{1}{h_2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_2}\hat{e}_2 + \frac{1}{h_3}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_3}\hat{e}_3.\]
Divergence: \[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{h_1 h_2 h_3}\left[\frac{\partial(h_2 h_3 F_1)}{\partial q_1} + \frac{\partial(h_1 h_3 F_2)}{\partial q_2} + \frac{\partial(h_1 h_2 F_3)}{\partial q_3}\right].\]
Curl: \[\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{h_1 h_2 h_3} \begin{vmatrix} h_1\hat{e}_1 & h_2\hat{e}_2 & h_3\hat{e}_3 \\ \partial_{q_1} & \partial_{q_2} & \partial_{q_3} \\ h_1 F_1 & h_2 F_2 & h_3 F_3 \end{vmatrix}.\]
Laplacian: \[\nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{h_1 h_2 h_3}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial q_1}\!\left(\frac{h_2 h_3}{h_1}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_1}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial q_2}\!\left(\frac{h_1 h_3}{h_2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_2}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial q_3}\!\left(\frac{h_1 h_2}{h_3}\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_3}\right)\right].\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 9.7-9.9 (operators in Cartesian); the general curvilinear derivation via scale factors is covered more fully in Taylor (2005), Ch. 16 (curvilinear coordinates).

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
text:
5.4 Operators in Spherical Coordinates
Substituting \((h_r, h_\theta, h_\phi) = (1, r, r\sin\theta)\):
Gradient: \[\nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\hat{r} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\hat{\theta} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi}\hat{\phi}.\]
Divergence: \[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial(r^2 F_r)}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial(\sin\theta\, F_\theta)}{\partial \theta} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial F_\phi}{\partial \phi}.\]
Curl: \[\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\!\left(\frac{\partial(\sin\theta\, F_\phi)}{\partial \theta} - \frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial \phi}\right)\hat{r} + \frac{1}{r}\!\left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial \phi} - \frac{\partial(r F_\phi)}{\partial r}\right)\hat{\theta} + \frac{1}{r}\!\left(\frac{\partial(r F_\theta)}{\partial r} - \frac{\partial F_r}{\partial \theta}\right)\hat{\phi}.\]
Laplacian: \[\nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(r^2\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\!\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \phi^2}.\]

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
text:
5.5 Laplace-Beltrami Operator on \(S^2\)
On the unit sphere (\(r = 1\), constant), only the angular part of the Laplacian survives. The Laplace-Beltrami operator is
\[\Delta_{S^2} f = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\!\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\right) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \phi^2}.\]
The full Laplacian decomposes as
\[\nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(r^2\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2}\Delta_{S^2} f.\]
\(\Delta_{S^2}\) is the operator whose eigenfunctions are the spherical harmonics.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 12.10 (Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates and the derivation of the spherical Laplacian); Evans (2010), Appendix C (notation and operator identities).

title: 5  Spherical Coordinates
text:
5.6 Worked Examples
Gradient of a radial function. Compute \(\nabla(r^2)\) in spherical coordinates.
\(f = r^2\) depends only on \(r\), so \(\partial f/\partial\theta = \partial f/\partial\phi = 0\):
\[\nabla(r^2) = \frac{\partial(r^2)}{\partial r}\hat{r} = 2r\hat{r}.\]
Consistent with the Cartesian result \(\nabla(x^2+y^2+z^2) = 2(x,y,z)\).

Divergence of a radial vector field. Let \(\mathbf{F} = r^2\hat{r}\). Compute \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}\).
Only the radial term contributes:
\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial(r^2 \cdot r^2)}{\partial r} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial r^4}{\partial r} = \frac{4r^3}{r^2} = 4r.\]

Fundamental solution of Laplace’s equation. Show \(\nabla^2(1/r) = 0\) for \(r \neq 0\).
\[\nabla^2\!\left(\frac{1}{r}\right) = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\!\left(r^2 \frac{d}{dr}\frac{1}{r}\right) = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\!\left(-1\right) = 0.\]
\(1/r\) is the fundamental solution of the Laplace equation in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) - the Green’s function for \(-\nabla^2\). Its angular average over any sphere centered at the origin is \(1/r\), constant on each sphere, which is why it is rotationally symmetric and satisfies \(\Delta_{S^2}(1/r) = 0\) trivially (no angular dependence).

Solid angle integral. Compute \(\int_{S^2} \cos^2\theta\, d\Omega\).
\[\int_{S^2} \cos^2\theta\, d\Omega = \int_0^{2\pi} d\phi \int_0^{\pi} \cos^2\theta\sin\theta\, d\theta = 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} u^2\, du = 2\pi \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3}.\]
The mean value of \(\cos^2\theta\) over \(S^2\) is \(\frac{1}{3}\), consistent with isotropy: \(\langle x^2\rangle = \langle y^2\rangle = \langle z^2\rangle = \langle r^2\rangle / 3\).




Evans, Lawrence C. 2010. Partial Differential Equations. 2nd ed. American Mathematical Society.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.


Taylor, John R. 2005. Classical Mechanics. University Science Books.

title: Harmonic Analysis
text: Fourier series and transforms describe functions through oscillatory bases. Spherical harmonics extend this construction to the sphere. The chapters develop the shared function-space theory, coefficients, convergence, and spectral identities used in numerical PDEs, fluid dynamics, and operator learning.

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.1 Vector Spaces
Before Fourier series or spherical harmonics can be stated precisely, we need the ambient space in which they live and the notion of convergence they satisfy. This section develops that theory abstractly. Fourier series and spherical harmonics are then special cases of a single general structure: an orthonormal basis for a Hilbert space.
Definition. A vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\) (or \(\mathbb{C}\)) is a set \(V\) equipped with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the usual axioms (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, identity, inverses).
The central examples here are spaces of functions:
The spaces \(C([a,b])\), \(C^k([a,b])\), and \(L^2([a,b])\) are infinite-dimensional. In contrast, \(\mathcal{P}_n\) has dimension \(n+1\), with basis \(1,x,\ldots,x^n\).

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
\(C([a,b])\): continuous functions on \([a,b]\), with pointwise operations.
\(C^k([a,b])\): \(k\)-times continuously differentiable functions.
\(\mathcal{P}_n\): polynomials of degree at most \(n\).
\(L^2([a,b])\): square-integrable functions (defined below).

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.2 Norms and \(L^p\) Spaces
Definition. A norm on a vector space \(V\) is a function \(\|\cdot\| : V \to [0,\infty)\) satisfying:

\(\|f\| = 0\) iff \(f = 0\).
\(\|\alpha f\| = |\alpha|\|f\|\).
\(\|f + g\| \leq \|f\| + \|g\|\) (triangle inequality).

A normed space is a vector space equipped with a norm.
Definition. For \(1 \leq p < \infty\), the \(L^p\) space on a domain \(\Omega\) is
\[L^p(\Omega) = \left\{ f : \Omega \to \mathbb{C} \;\Big|\; \int_\Omega |f(x)|^p\, dx < \infty \right\},\]
with norm \(\|f\|_p = \left(\int_\Omega |f|^p\, dx\right)^{1/p}\). Functions equal almost everywhere are identified.
The case \(p = 2\) is by far the most important for harmonic analysis:
\[L^2(\Omega) = \left\{ f : \Omega \to \mathbb{C} \;\Big|\; \int_\Omega |f(x)|^2\, dx < \infty \right\}, \quad \|f\|_2 = \left(\int_\Omega |f|^2\right)^{1/2}.\]
\(L^2\) is the natural space for energy: \(\|f\|_2^2\) is the total “energy” of \(f\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.5 (function spaces in the context of Sturm-Liouville); Evans (2010), Appendix E (\(L^p\) spaces).

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.3 Inner Product Spaces
Definition. An inner product on a vector space \(V\) is a map \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle : V \times V \to \mathbb{C}\) satisfying:

\(\langle f, f\rangle \geq 0\), with \(\langle f,f\rangle = 0\) iff \(f = 0\).
\(\langle f, g\rangle = \overline{\langle g, f\rangle}\) (conjugate symmetry).
\(\langle \alpha f + \beta g, h\rangle = \alpha\langle f,h\rangle + \beta\langle g,h\rangle\) (linearity in first argument).

The inner product induces a norm: \(\|f\| = \sqrt{\langle f,f\rangle}\).
On \(L^2(\Omega)\):
\[\langle f, g\rangle = \int_\Omega f(x)\,\overline{g(x)}\, dx.\]
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. For any \(f, g \in V\):
\[|\langle f, g\rangle| \leq \|f\|\,\|g\|.\]
Equality holds iff \(f\) and \(g\) are proportional. This is the generalization of the dot product inequality \(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\) to infinite dimensions.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.5.

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.4 Hilbert Spaces
A normed space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges to an element of the space. Completeness is the key property that allows infinite series to be controlled.
Definition. A Hilbert space is a complete inner product space.
Key example. \(L^2(\Omega)\) is a Hilbert space. This is not obvious: it requires showing that limits of \(L^2\)-Cauchy sequences are again in \(L^2\). The pointwise limit of a sequence of \(L^2\) functions need not be the \(L^2\) limit.
\(C([a,b])\) with the \(L^2\) norm is an inner product space but is not complete (the limit of a Cauchy sequence of continuous functions can be discontinuous). Completing it gives \(L^2([a,b])\).
Intuition. A Hilbert space is an infinite-dimensional generalization of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with dot product. Virtually all geometric intuitions from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) carry over: projections, angles, decompositions into orthogonal components.
Further reading: Evans (2010), Appendix E; Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.6.

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.5 Orthogonality
Definition. \(f, g \in V\) are orthogonal if \(\langle f, g\rangle = 0\), written \(f \perp g\). A set \(\{e_n\}\) is:

Orthogonal if \(\langle e_n, e_m\rangle = 0\) for \(n \neq m\).
Orthonormal if additionally \(\langle e_n, e_n\rangle = 1\) for all \(n\).

Pythagorean theorem. If \(f \perp g\), then \(\|f + g\|^2 = \|f\|^2 + \|g\|^2\).
More generally, for a finite orthonormal set \(\{e_1, \ldots, e_N\}\) and coefficients \(c_n = \langle f, e_n\rangle\):
\[\left\|f - \sum_{n=1}^N c_n e_n\right\|^2 = \|f\|^2 - \sum_{n=1}^N |c_n|^2.\]
The partial sum \(\sum c_n e_n\) is the orthogonal projection of \(f\) onto \(\text{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_N\}\), and is the best approximation to \(f\) in that subspace.
Gram-Schmidt process. Any countable linearly independent set \(\{f_n\}\) can be orthonormalized: set \(e_1 = f_1/\|f_1\|\), then iteratively subtract the projection onto the span of previous \(e_k\) and normalize.

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.6 Orthonormal Bases and Fourier Coefficients
Definition. An orthonormal set \(\{e_n\}_{n=1}^\infty\) in a Hilbert space \(H\) is an orthonormal basis (or complete orthonormal system) if the only element orthogonal to every \(e_n\) is zero:
\[\langle f, e_n\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } n \implies f = 0.\]
Equivalently, \(\{e_n\}\) is an ONB iff every \(f \in H\) expands as
\[f = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle f, e_n\rangle\, e_n,\]
where the sum converges in the norm of \(H\) (not necessarily pointwise). The coefficients \(\hat{f}_n = \langle f, e_n\rangle\) are the generalized Fourier coefficients of \(f\) with respect to \(\{e_n\}\).
Bessel’s inequality. For any ONS (not necessarily a basis) and any \(f \in H\):
\[\sum_n |\langle f, e_n\rangle|^2 \leq \|f\|^2.\]
Parseval’s identity. If \(\{e_n\}\) is an ONB:
\[\sum_n |\langle f, e_n\rangle|^2 = \|f\|^2.\]
Parseval says the ONB is “complete”: no energy is lost in the decomposition. It is equivalent to the ONB condition.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.6 (generalized Fourier series, Parseval); Evans (2010), Appendix E.

title: 6  Function Spaces
text:
6.7 Sturm-Liouville Theory
Orthogonal function families do not arise by accident. They are the eigenfunctions of self-adjoint differential operators - a general principle captured by Sturm-Liouville theory.
The Sturm-Liouville problem. On \([a,b]\), with weight function \(w(x) > 0\):
\[-\frac{d}{dx}\!\left(p(x)\frac{df}{dx}\right) + q(x)f = \lambda\, w(x)\, f, \qquad \text{(with boundary conditions)}.\]
Theorem. Under mild regularity conditions, the Sturm-Liouville problem has:

A countable set of real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \to \infty\).
Eigenfunctions \(\{f_n\}\) that are orthogonal in the weighted \(L^2\) space with inner product \(\langle f, g\rangle_w = \int_a^b f(x)\overline{g(x)}\, w(x)\, dx\).
The eigenfunctions form a complete orthonormal basis for \(L^2_w([a,b])\).

Connection to specific bases:








Problem
Operator
Eigenfunctions

Fourier series and spherical harmonic expansions are eigenfunction expansions of self-adjoint operators. Separating the spherical problem gives associated Legendre equations, which are singular Sturm-Liouville problems with endpoint regularity conditions; the sphere is not itself a one-dimensional interval problem.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.5 (Sturm-Liouville problems and orthogonal functions) and Sec. 12.10 (spherical harmonics as the Sturm-Liouville problem on \(S^2\)).




Evans, Lawrence C. 2010. Partial Differential Equations. 2nd ed. American Mathematical Society.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 7  Fourier Series
text:
7.1 Definition and Coefficients
The Fourier series is the concrete realization of the abstract ONB expansion from the function spaces section, applied to \(L^2([-\pi,\pi])\). The basis is the family of complex exponentials \(e^{inx}\), which are the eigenfunctions of \(-d^2/dx^2\) with periodic boundary conditions - a Sturm-Liouville problem on \([-\pi,\pi]\).
The functions \(\phi_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{inx}\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), form an orthonormal basis for \(L^2([-\pi,\pi])\) under the inner product \(\langle f,g\rangle = \int_{-\pi}^\pi f\bar{g}\, dx\).
Definition. The Fourier series of \(f \in L^2([-\pi, \pi])\) is
\[f(x) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n\, e^{inx}, \qquad c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\, e^{-inx}\, dx.\]
With this normalized basis, \(\langle f, \phi_n\rangle = \sqrt{2\pi}\,c_n\). Thus \(f = \sum_n \langle f,\phi_n\rangle\phi_n = \sum_n c_n e^{inx}\). The series converges in \(L^2\); Parseval’s identity gives \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi |f|^2\,dx = \sum_n |c_n|^2\).
Real form. For real \(f\), writing \(e^{inx} = \cos(nx) + i\sin(nx)\):
\[f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigl(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\bigr),\]
where \(a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\, dx\) and \(b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\, dx\).
Example. Let \(f(x) = x\) on \([-\pi, \pi]\). Then \(a_n = 0\) (odd function) and \(b_n = \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\):
\[x = 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin(nx) = 2\left(\sin x - \frac{\sin 2x}{2} + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} - \cdots\right).\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Secs. 11.1-11.2; Brunton and Kutz (2022), Sec. 2.1.

title: 7  Fourier Series
text:
7.2 Convergence
For \(f \in L^2\), the Fourier series converges in mean square but need not converge pointwise everywhere. Key results:

If \(f\) is piecewise smooth, the series converges to \(f(x)\) at continuity points and to \(\frac{1}{2}[f(x^+) + f(x^-)]\) at jump discontinuities (Gibbs phenomenon near jumps).
If \(f \in C^k\), then \(|c_n| = O(n^{-k})\): smoother functions have faster-decaying coefficients.

Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.1 (convergence discussion).

title: 7  Fourier Series
text:
7.3 Worked Example: Square Wave
Let \(f\) be the \(2\pi\)-periodic square wave:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & 0 < x < \pi \\ -1 & -\pi < x < 0 \end{cases}.\]
Since \(f\) is odd, all cosine coefficients vanish: \(a_n = 0\). For the sine coefficients:
\[b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\, dx = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\sin(nx)\, dx = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[-\frac{\cos(nx)}{n}\right]_0^{\pi} = \frac{2}{n\pi}(1 - \cos(n\pi)).\]
Since \(\cos(n\pi) = (-1)^n\):
\[b_n = \frac{2}{n\pi}(1 - (-1)^n) = \begin{cases} 4/(n\pi) & n \text{ odd} \\ 0 & n \text{ even} \end{cases}.\]
The Fourier series is
\[f(x) = \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\sin((2k+1)x)}{2k+1} = \frac{4}{\pi}\left(\sin x + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} + \frac{\sin 5x}{5} + \cdots\right).\]
The coefficients decay as \(O(1/n)\), consistent with jump discontinuities: this square wave is not continuous. Near each jump, the limiting overshoot is approximately \(9\%\) of the jump height, or \(18\%\) of the unit plateau magnitude (Gibbs phenomenon).




Brunton, Steven L., and J. Nathan Kutz. 2022. Data-Driven Science and Engineering: Machine Learning, Dynamical Systems, and Control. 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 8  Fourier Transform
text:
8.1 Definition
The Fourier transform extends Fourier series to functions on \(\mathbb{R}\), replacing the discrete sum over frequencies with a continuous integral.
Definition. For \(f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})\), the Fourier transform is
\[\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i \xi x}\, dx.\]
The inverse Fourier transform recovers \(f\) from \(\hat{f}\):
\[f(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\xi)\, e^{2\pi i \xi x}\, d\xi.\]
\(\hat{f}(\xi)\) is the amplitude of the frequency component \(\xi\) in \(f\). The transform is well-defined and invertible for \(f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\) (Plancherel theorem).
Alternative convention. With angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi\xi\):
\[\hat{f}(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-i\omega x}\, dx, \qquad f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\omega)\, e^{i\omega x}\, d\omega.\]
Both conventions are standard; the choice affects normalization factors.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.7 (Fourier integral) and Sec. 11.9 (Fourier transform); Brunton and Kutz (2022), Sec. 2.1.

title: 8  Fourier Transform
text:
8.2 Key Properties
Let \(\mathcal{F}[f] = \hat{f}\).
Linearity: \(\mathcal{F}[\alpha f + \beta g] = \alpha\hat{f} + \beta\hat{g}\).
Shift: \(\mathcal{F}[f(x - a)](\xi) = e^{-2\pi i \xi a}\hat{f}(\xi)\). Shifting in space is multiplication by a phase in frequency.
Derivative: \(\mathcal{F}[f^{(n)}](\xi) = (2\pi i \xi)^n \hat{f}(\xi)\). Differentiation in space is multiplication by \(i\xi\) in frequency. This is the key property that converts differential equations into algebraic equations.
Convolution theorem: For \((f * g)(x) = \int f(y)\, g(x-y)\, dy\):
\[\mathcal{F}[f * g] = \hat{f} \cdot \hat{g}.\]
Convolution in the spatial domain is pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain.
Parseval / Plancherel:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(x)|^2\, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |\hat{f}(\xi)|^2\, d\xi.\]
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.9 (properties and convolution theorem).

title: 8  Fourier Transform
text:
8.3 Differential Equations via Fourier Transform
The derivative property makes the Fourier transform a natural tool for solving linear PDEs with constant coefficients. Applying \(\mathcal{F}\) converts \(\partial_x \to 2\pi i\xi\), turning a PDE into an algebraic equation in frequency space.
Example. Solve \(f'(x) + af(x) = g(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Taking the Fourier transform:
\[(2\pi i\xi + a)\hat{f}(\xi) = \hat{g}(\xi) \implies \hat{f}(\xi) = \frac{\hat{g}(\xi)}{2\pi i\xi + a}.\]
Inverting gives \(f = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\hat{g}/(2\pi i\xi + a)]\). This solution is a convolution \(f = g * h\) where \(h = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[1/(2\pi i\xi + a)]\) is the impulse response - the Green’s function of the operator \(\partial_x + a\).
Further reading: Evans (2010), Ch. 4 (Fourier transform applied to PDEs, Green’s functions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

title: 8  Fourier Transform
text:
8.4 Discrete Fourier Transform
For a finite sequence \(x_0, \ldots, x_{N-1}\), the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is
\[X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2\pi i kn/N}, \qquad k = 0, \ldots, N-1.\]
The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) computes the DFT in \(O(N\log N)\) rather than \(O(N^2)\). The convolution theorem holds exactly for the DFT, making the FFT the computational backbone of spectral methods and the Fourier Neural Operator.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 11.9 (DFT and FFT); Brunton and Kutz (2022), Sec. 2.2 (FFT and applications in data-driven methods).

title: 8  Fourier Transform
text:
8.5 Key Identities: Derivations
All derivations below use the convention \(\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx\).

8.5.1 Derivative Property
Claim. \(\mathcal{F}[f^{(n)}](\xi) = (2\pi i\xi)^n \hat{f}(\xi)\).
Derivation (n=1). Integrate by parts, assuming \(f(x) \to 0\) as \(|x| \to \infty\):
\[\mathcal{F}[f'](\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f'(x)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx = \underbrace{\left[f(x) e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}}_{= 0} + 2\pi i\xi \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx = 2\pi i\xi\, \hat{f}(\xi).\]
Applying the same identity \(n\) times gives the general result. Differentiation in the spatial domain is multiplication by \(2\pi i\xi\) in the frequency domain, converting a differential operator into an algebraic one.



8.5.2 Convolution Theorem
Claim. \(\mathcal{F}[f * g](\xi) = \hat{f}(\xi)\cdot\hat{g}(\xi)\).
Derivation. Write out the transform of the convolution and swap the order of integration (Fubini):
\[\mathcal{F}[f * g](\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y)\, g(x-y)\, dy\right) e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y) \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x-y)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx\right) dy.\]
Substitute \(u = x - y\) in the inner integral (\(du = dx\), \(x = u + y\)):
\[= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y) \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi(u+y)}\, du\right) dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi y}\, dy \cdot \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi u}\, du = \hat{f}(\xi)\cdot\hat{g}(\xi).\]
The reverse direction also holds: pointwise multiplication in frequency corresponds to convolution in space, \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}[\hat{f}\cdot\hat{g}] = f * g\). This is the basis for the FNO: learned filters applied in the frequency domain correspond to convolution operators in the spatial domain.



8.5.3 Gaussian Identity
Claim. For \(a > 0\): \(\mathcal{F}[e^{-\pi a x^2}](\xi) = a^{-1/2}\, e^{-\pi \xi^2/a}\).
In particular, \(\mathcal{F}[e^{-\pi x^2}] = e^{-\pi\xi^2}\): the standard Gaussian is a fixed point of the Fourier transform.
Derivation. Let \(I(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\pi a x^2} e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx\). Complete the square in the exponent:
\[-\pi a x^2 - 2\pi i\xi x = -\pi a\!\left(x + \frac{i\xi}{a}\right)^2 - \frac{\pi\xi^2}{a}.\]
Factoring out the \(\xi\)-dependent constant:
\[I(\xi) = e^{-\pi\xi^2/a} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\pi a(x + i\xi/a)^2}\, dx.\]
The substitution \(u = \sqrt{a}(x + i\xi/a)\) (shifting the contour in the complex plane, justified by analyticity) gives \(du = \sqrt{a}\, dx\) and:
\[I(\xi) = e^{-\pi\xi^2/a} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\pi u^2}\, du = \frac{e^{-\pi\xi^2/a}}{\sqrt{a}},\]
using the Gaussian integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\pi u^2}\, du = 1\).
The Gaussian plays a central role in analysis because it is maximally concentrated simultaneously in space and frequency (saturating the uncertainty principle), and because it is self-dual under the Fourier transform.



8.5.4 Dirac Delta
The Dirac delta \(\delta(x)\) is the distribution satisfying \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x)\, f(x)\, dx = f(0)\) for any test function \(f\).
Claim. \(\mathcal{F}[\delta](\xi) = 1\) and \(\mathcal{F}[1](\xi) = \delta(\xi)\).
Derivation of \(\mathcal{F}[\delta] = 1\).
\[\hat{\delta}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x)\, e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\, dx = e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot 0} = 1.\]
A point mass in space has equal energy at all frequencies - a flat spectrum. This is the distributional analogue of the impulse response: the Green’s function of a differential operator \(L\) is the function \(G\) satisfying \(LG = \delta\), and in frequency space this becomes \(\hat{L}(\xi)\hat{G}(\xi) = 1\), so \(\hat{G}(\xi) = 1/\hat{L}(\xi)\).
Shifted delta. \(\mathcal{F}[\delta(\cdot - a)](\xi) = e^{-2\pi i\xi a}\). A pure spatial shift is a linear phase in frequency.




Brunton, Steven L., and J. Nathan Kutz. 2022. Data-Driven Science and Engineering: Machine Learning, Dynamical Systems, and Control. 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.


Evans, Lawrence C. 2010. Partial Differential Equations. 2nd ed. American Mathematical Society.


Kreyszig, Erwin. 2011. Advanced Engineering Mathematics. 10th ed. Wiley.

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.1 Definition
The spherical harmonics are the eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator \(\Delta_{S^2}\) on \(S^2\), playing the role of \(e^{inx}\) on the sphere. They are the instance of the Sturm-Liouville framework (see the function spaces section) for the operator \(-\Delta_{S^2}\) with the standard \(L^2(S^2)\) inner product.
In spherical coordinates \((\theta, \phi)\) with \(\theta \in [0,\pi]\) (colatitude) and \(\phi \in [0, 2\pi)\) (longitude), the spherical harmonics are
\[Y_l^m(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{(2l+1)}{4\pi}\frac{(l-m)!}{(l+m)!}}\, P_l^m(\cos\theta)\, e^{im\phi},\]
where \(l = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) is the degree, \(m = -l, \ldots, l\) is the order, and \(P_l^m\) are the associated Legendre functions with the Condon–Shortley phase. For \(m\ge0\), \(P_l^m(t)=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}d^mP_l(t)/dt^m\). Negative orders obey \(Y_l^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{Y_l^m}\). There are \(2l+1\) harmonics of each degree, and infinitely many degrees.
Eigenvalue equation. The spherical harmonics satisfy
\[\Delta_{S^2} Y_l^m = -l(l+1)\, Y_l^m.\]
The eigenvalue \(-l(l+1)\) depends only on degree \(l\), not order \(m\): each eigenspace has dimension \(2l+1\).
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Secs. 12.10-12.11 (Laplace’s equation in spherical coordinates, Legendre polynomials, and associated Legendre functions).

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.2 Orthogonality and Completeness
The \(\{Y_l^m\}\) form an ONB for \(L^2(S^2)\) in the sense of the function spaces section. The specific orthonormality relation is
\[\int_{S^2} Y_l^m(\theta,\phi)\, \overline{Y_{l'}^{m'}(\theta,\phi)}\, d\Omega = \delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'},\]
where \(d\Omega = \sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi\). The expansion and Parseval identity follow from the general ONB theory:
\[f(\theta,\phi) = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}\sum_{m=-l}^{l} \hat{f}_l^m\, Y_l^m(\theta,\phi), \qquad \hat{f}_l^m = \int_{S^2} f\, \overline{Y_l^m}\, d\Omega, \qquad \int_{S^2} |f|^2\, d\Omega = \sum_{l,m} |\hat{f}_l^m|^2.\]
This is the spherical harmonic transform, the analogue of the Fourier series on \(S^2\). Its numerical evaluation, Gaussian grids, and sampling conditions are developed in spectral numerical methods.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 12.11 (orthogonality of Legendre polynomials, basis for the expansion).

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.3 Low-degree Examples

\(Y_0^0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\): constant function, \(l=0\).
\(Y_1^0 = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\cos\theta\): proportional to \(z/r\), the north-south dipole.
\(Y_1^{\pm 1} = \mp\sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\sin\theta\, e^{\pm i\phi}\): equatorial dipoles.

Degree \(l\) sets the Laplacian eigenvalue and an angular scale of order \(1/l\) for large \(l\). The order \(m\) sets the longitude dependence. A single oscillation count does not describe every harmonic at fixed degree.

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.4 Addition Theorem
For any two directions \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}, \hat{\mathbf{r}}' \in S^2\) with angle \(\gamma\) between them:
\[P_l(\cos\gamma) = \frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\sum_{m=-l}^{l} Y_l^m(\hat{\mathbf{r}})\, \overline{Y_l^m(\hat{\mathbf{r}}')},\]
where \(P_l\) is the Legendre polynomial of degree \(l\). This identity is used to express rotationally symmetric kernels (such as Green’s functions on \(S^2\)) in terms of spherical harmonics.
Further reading: Kreyszig (2011), Sec. 12.11 (Legendre polynomials and their properties).

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.5 Convolution on \(S^2\)
A rotationally symmetric kernel \(K(\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}}')\) (depending only on the angle between two points) acts by convolution on the sphere. By the addition theorem, convolution with such a kernel is diagonal in the spherical harmonic basis: each coefficient \(\hat{f}_l^m\) is multiplied by a degree-dependent factor \(\hat{K}_l\). This diagonalization applies to rotationally symmetric kernels. More general position-dependent kernels need not act diagonally in this basis.
Further reading: Tang et al. (2026) (GSNO paper, Sec. 2-3, where this diagonalization is the direct basis for the architecture); Bonev et al. (2023) (Sec. 2, spherical harmonic convolution in the SFNO).

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
text:
9.6 Worked Example: Expanding \(\cos^2\theta\)
Expand \(f(\theta, \phi) = \cos^2\theta\) in spherical harmonics.
Since \(f\) is independent of \(\phi\), only \(m = 0\) terms appear. Write \(\cos^2\theta\) in terms of Legendre polynomials using the identity \(P_2(t) = \frac{1}{2}(3t^2 - 1)\), so \(t^2 = \frac{1}{3}(2P_2(t) + 1)\):
\[\cos^2\theta = \frac{1}{3}(2P_2(\cos\theta) + P_0(\cos\theta)).\]
Converting to spherical harmonics with \(Y_l^0 = \sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}} P_l(\cos\theta)\):
\[P_0(\cos\theta) = \sqrt{4\pi}\, Y_0^0, \qquad P_2(\cos\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{5}}\, Y_2^0.\]
Substituting:
\[\cos^2\theta = \frac{\sqrt{4\pi}}{3}\, Y_0^0 + \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{5}}\, Y_2^0.\]
Only \(l = 0\) and \(l = 2\) components are nonzero. This is expected: \(\cos^2\theta\) is a degree-2 polynomial in \(\cos\theta\), and the \(l\)-th spherical harmonic captures exactly degree-\(l\) angular structure.

title: 9  Spherical Harmonics
section: 9.7 Worked Example: Verifying the Eigenvalue Equation
text:
9.7 Worked Example: Verifying the Eigenvalue Equation
Verify \(\Delta_{S^2} Y_1^0 = -2\, Y_1^0\) directly, where \(Y_1^0(\theta,\phi) = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\theta\).
Since \(Y_1^0\) is independent of \(\phi\), the \(\partial_\phi^2\) term vanishes:
\[\Delta_{S^2} Y_1^0 = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\!\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\cos\theta\right) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(-\sin^2\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\frac{-2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = -2\,Y_1^0.\]
This confirms \(\Delta_{S^2} Y_1^0 = -l(l+1)\, Y_1^0 = -1\cdot 2\, Y_1^0\).

title: Partial Differential Equations
text:
Differential operators, boundary conditions, and forcing determine a PDE problem. Laplace and Poisson equations provide examples of Green’s functions and spectral solution methods. On the sphere, spherical harmonics connect these ideas to the Laplace-Beltrami operator.
The spectral methods chapter develops projection, Gaussian quadrature, spherical harmonic transforms, elliptic inversion, and nonlinear dealiasing.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.1 From a PDE to coefficient equations
A spectral method approximates a field by a finite sum of global basis functions. It solves for their coefficients rather than for independent values in each cell. The basis should respect the domain: Fourier modes suit periodic intervals, orthogonal polynomials suit bounded intervals, and spherical harmonics suit the sphere. The function-space chapter explains projection; here we turn projection into a numerical method.
Let \(u(x,t)\) be a scalar field on a domain \(D\), and let \(\{\varphi_j\}\) be an orthonormal basis for a specified inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). For \(J\) retained functions, write
\[
u_J(x,t)=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}a_j(t)\varphi_j(x).
\]
For a PDE \(\partial_t u=\mathcal{L}u+\mathcal{N}(u)+g\), a Galerkin method requires the residual to be orthogonal to every retained basis function:
\[
\frac{da_i}{dt}
=\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\langle\mathcal{L}\varphi_j,\varphi_i\rangle a_j
+\langle\mathcal{N}(u_J),\varphi_i\rangle
+\langle g,\varphi_i\rangle.
\]
Here \(\mathcal{L}\) is linear, \(\mathcal{N}\) contains nonlinear terms, and \(g\) is forcing. A nonorthonormal basis introduces a mass matrix \(M_{ij}=\langle\varphi_j,\varphi_i\rangle\) on the left. Boundary conditions must be built into the basis or imposed separately. A collocation method instead sets the residual to zero at selected nodes. A pseudospectral method evaluates terms through transformations between coefficients and node values. With adequate quadrature and dealiasing, its computed nonlinear projection can agree with Galerkin projection. These distinctions concern spatial discretization; time integration is a separate numerical choice. See Boyd (2001) for the general framework.
For a periodic interval \([0,2\pi)\), \(\partial_x e^{ikx}=ik e^{ikx}\) and \(\partial_x^2e^{ikx}=-k^2e^{ikx}\). Differentiation becomes coefficient multiplication. With physical coordinate \(s=Rx\), the derivative is instead \(\partial_s=R^{-1}\partial_x\), so its units are inverse length.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
section: 10.2 Why global expansions can be accurate
text:
10.2 Why global expansions can be accurate
For an orthonormal basis, the squared \(L^2\) truncation error is the energy in omitted coefficients. Rapid coefficient decay therefore gives rapid convergence. For periodic analytic functions that extend analytically into a complex strip, Fourier coefficients decay exponentially with mode number. Finite regularity usually gives algebraic decay. Discontinuities cause oscillations near jumps and slow convergence; increasing the truncation alone does not remove the Gibbs phenomenon. Spectral accuracy depends on regularity and compatible boundary conditions, not merely on choosing a transform.
A global method is useful when smooth solutions need high accuracy, derivatives or elliptic inversions have simple coefficient formulas, or scale-dependent analysis is central. Local methods may be preferable for shocks, complex boundaries, local refinement, or localized communication.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.3 Spherical harmonic representation
Use colatitude \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\), longitude \(\phi\in[0,2\pi)\), latitude \(\alpha=\pi/2-\theta\), and radius \(R>0\) in metres. Define \(\mu=\cos\theta=\sin\alpha\). Solid angle is dimensionless:
\[
d\Omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=d\mu\,d\phi
\]
when the \(\mu\) integral runs from \(-1\) to \(1\). Physical area is \(R^2d\Omega\). Use the orthonormal complex harmonics from the spherical harmonics chapter. For \(m\ge0\), their associated Legendre functions include the Condon–Shortley phase:
\[
P_\ell^m(\mu)=(-1)^m(1-\mu^2)^{m/2}
\frac{d^mP_\ell}{d\mu^m},
\qquad
Y_\ell^m=N_{\ell m}P_\ell^m(\mu)e^{im\phi},
\quad
N_{\ell m}=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}\frac{(\ell-m)!}{(\ell+m)!}}.
\]
Negative orders satisfy \(Y_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{Y_\ell^m}\). Triangular truncation at degree \(L\) retains
\[
f_L=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}
\widehat f_\ell^mY_\ell^m,
\qquad
\widehat f_\ell^m=\int_{S^2}f\overline{Y_\ell^m}\,d\Omega.
\]
There are \((L+1)^2\) complex basis functions. A real field obeys \(\widehat f_\ell^{-m}=(-1)^m\overline{\widehat f_\ell^m}\), reducing independent storage. If \(f\) has units \(U\), so do its coefficients under this dimensionless normalization. Truncation degree and the number of stored modes differ by one when degree zero is included.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.4 Gaussian grid and quadrature
A quadrature rule approximates an integral by weighted function values. The \(n\)-point Gauss–Legendre rule on \([-1,1]\) uses the roots \(\mu_i\) of the Legendre polynomial \(P_n\) and positive weights
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}q(\mu)\,d\mu
\approx\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iq(\mu_i),
\qquad
w_i=\frac{2}{(1-\mu_i^2)[P_n'(\mu_i)]^2}.
\]
It is exact for polynomials of degree at most \(2n-1\), and \(\sum_iw_i=2\). Golub and Welsch (1969) gives algorithms for computing Gaussian rules from orthogonal-polynomial recurrences. The following argument explains why the Legendre nodes give this exactness.
For a polynomial \(q\) of degree at most \(2n-1\), polynomial division gives \(q=P_ns+r\), where \(s\) and \(r\) have degree at most \(n-1\). Legendre orthogonality makes \(\int P_ns=0\). At every node \(P_n(\mu_i)=0\), so \(q(\mu_i)=r(\mu_i)\). Choose weights that integrate the Lagrange interpolant of \(r\) exactly. The same weighted sum then integrates \(q\) exactly. The extra exact degrees come from orthogonality, not from uniformly spacing the nodes.
A full Gaussian grid combines these nodes with \(M\) equally spaced longitudes:
\[
\alpha_i=\arcsin\mu_i,\qquad
\phi_j=\frac{2\pi j}{M},\quad j=0,\ldots,M-1.
\]
Latitudes are not equally spaced, and no node is at a pole. An equatorial node exists when \(n\) is odd. Every latitude ring has the same \(M\) longitudes; a reduced Gaussian grid instead varies their count and needs a corresponding transform algorithm. The full-grid formulas below do not apply unchanged to a reduced grid.
The area integral and global mean are approximated by
\[
\int_{S_R^2}f\,dA
\approx R^2\frac{2\pi}{M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij},
\qquad
\langle f\rangle_A\approx\frac{1}{2M}\sum_{i,j}w_if_{ij}.
\]
Thus a constant integrates to \(4\pi R^2\). For a zonal profile, normalized latitude weights are \(w_i/2\). Do not multiply Gaussian weights by \(\cos\alpha_i\) again: the substitution \(d\mu=\cos\alpha\,d\alpha\) already accounts for the area Jacobian. Uniform weights per latitude ring would also be incorrect.

10.4.1 Worked quadrature example
For \(n=2\), the nodes are \(\mu=\pm1/\sqrt3\) and both weights are one. For \(f=\mu^2\) the approximate global mean is
\[
\frac12\left[\left(-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2+
\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2\right]=\frac13,
\]
which equals \(\frac12\int_{-1}^{1}\mu^2\,d\mu\). The same rule gives \(1/9\) for the mean of \(\mu^4\), whereas its exact mean is \(1/5\). Degree four exceeds this rule’s degree-three guarantee.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
section: 10.5 Why this grid helps the SHT
text:
10.5 Why this grid helps the SHT
The spherical harmonic transform (SHT) separates into longitude Fourier analysis and latitude Legendre analysis. For \(m\ge0\), define
\[
F_m(\mu_i)=\frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}f(\mu_i,\phi_j)e^{-im\phi_j}.
\]
Then compute
\[
\widehat f_\ell^m\approx
2\pi N_{\ell m}\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iF_m(\mu_i)P_\ell^m(\mu_i).
\]
An FFT computes all longitude coefficients on each ring. Associated Legendre sums complete the forward transform; synthesis evaluates the harmonic sum at nodes. See Schaeffer (2013) for a practical transform algorithm.
For a field bandlimited to degree \(L\), sufficient sampling conditions for exact coefficient recovery in exact arithmetic are
\[
n\ge L+1,\qquad M\ge 2L+1.
\]
To see why, expand the input in retained harmonics. The longitude sum contains \(e^{i(m'-m)\phi_j}\) and is zero unless \(m'=m\) under this sampling condition. For the surviving terms,
\[
P_\ell^m(\mu)P_{\ell'}^m(\mu)
=(1-\mu^2)^m\frac{d^mP_\ell}{d\mu^m}
\frac{d^mP_{\ell'}}{d\mu^m},
\]
which is a polynomial of degree at most \(\ell+\ell'\le2L\). Since \(2n-1\ge2L\), Gaussian quadrature integrates these products exactly. The discrete inner product therefore reproduces orthogonality on the retained harmonic space. This is why the nodes and weights are part of the transform definition.
The statement does not claim that each \(P_\ell^m\) is itself a polynomial: odd \(m\) introduces a square root. The same-order product is polynomial. Nor does it promise exact coefficients for arbitrary sampled fields with energy above \(L\). Such unresolved structure can alias into retained modes.
For the bandlimited field, discrete Parseval also follows:
\[
\frac{2\pi}{M}\sum_{i,j}w_i|f_L(\mu_i,\phi_j)|^2
=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\sum_{m=-\ell}^{\ell}|\widehat f_\ell^m|^2.
\]
Round trips and this identity test normalization, weights, and coordinate order. Reversing latitude requires reversing the data and weights together. A shifted longitude origin requires consistent Fourier phases. Shape agreement alone does not establish transform compatibility.
A direct separated implementation uses approximately \(O(nM\log M)\) work for longitude FFTs and \(O(nL^2)\) for the Legendre stage. For \(n,M=O(L)\) the latter is cubic. An SHT is not simply a two-dimensional FFT. Recurrences, symmetry, precomputation, and specialized algorithms change practical costs and memory needs.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.6 Solving equations in spectral space
On a radius-\(R\) sphere, the physical Laplace–Beltrami operator satisfies
\[
\Delta_{S_R^2}Y_\ell^m=-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2}Y_\ell^m.
\]
For Poisson’s equation \(\Delta_{S_R^2}u=f\), the sphere has no boundary and a constant is in the nullspace. A solution exists only when \(\int f\,d\Omega=0\). Fix the undetermined mean by setting \(\widehat u_0^0=0\). For every \(\ell\ge1\),
\[
\widehat u_\ell^m=-\frac{R^2}{\ell(\ell+1)}\widehat f_\ell^m.
\]
For example, if \(f=A Y_2^0\), then \(u=-AR^2Y_2^0/6\). Applying the Laplacian recovers \(f\), checking the sign and radius factor. If \(f\) has units \(U\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\), \(u\) has units \(U\).
For diffusion \(\partial_t u=\kappa\Delta_{S_R^2}u\), with diffusivity \(\kappa\) in \(\mathrm{m}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1}\),
\[
\widehat u_\ell^m(t)=\widehat u_\ell^m(0)
\exp\left[-\frac{\kappa\ell(\ell+1)}{R^2}t\right].
\]
The mean remains constant and smaller scales decay faster. If forward Euler is used instead of this exact update, stability for all retained diffusion modes requires \(\Delta t\le2R^2/[\kappa L(L+1)]\) for \(L\ge1\). Accurate spatial differentiation does not remove time-step restrictions.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.7 Nonlinear terms and aliasing
A product of fields bandlimited to \(L\) can contain degrees up to \(2L\). Computing it on the minimally sampled grid and transforming back can fold unresolved modes into lower degrees. In a periodic example, grid samples cannot distinguish Fourier modes \(k\) and \(k+M\) because \(e^{i(k+M)2\pi j/M}=e^{ik2\pi j/M}\).
For exact projection of a product of two scalar degree-\(L\) fields onto degrees through \(L\), a sufficient full Gaussian grid satisfies
\[
M>3L,\qquad 2n-1\ge3L.
\]
The longitude integrand contains three mode factors. Its maximum frequency is \(3L\). Surviving latitude products also have degree at most \(3L\): the longitude selection rule makes the sum of their absolute orders even, so the factors of \((1-\mu^2)^{1/2}\) combine into an integer power. Gaussian exactness then applies. This is the spherical counterpart of padding each dimension by roughly \(3/2\) for a quadratic product. Strict inequalities and integer rounding matter. Derivatives of vector components and higher-order nonlinearities require their own analysis; these bounds apply to scalar products as stated.
A pseudospectral step therefore synthesizes on an adequate grid, evaluates the nonlinear expression there, analyzes it, and retains only the intended modes. Filtering damps selected coefficients but does not retroactively make an aliased projection exact. Dealiasing, physical diffusion, and numerical filtering serve different purposes.

title: 10  Spectral numerical methods
text:
10.8 Uses and numerical checks
Spectral coefficients support elliptic inversion, diffusion, scale-dependent filtering, energy spectra, and comparison across resolutions. A scalar isotropic linear filter multiplies all orders at degree \(\ell\) by the same factor; this preserves rotational symmetry. General position-dependent coefficients couple modes and need not yield diagonal operators.
Before using a transform in a solver, verify a constant, an individual harmonic, a forward/inverse round trip, and discrete Parseval. Check an analytic PDE solution such as the diffusion mode above. Increase truncation and quadrature resolution separately: convergence in one does not demonstrate convergence in the other. Record basis normalization, phase convention, radius, retained degrees, node coordinates, and weights so that stored coefficients remain interpretable.

title: Geophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
The sequence derives the stochastically stirred barotropic vorticity equation from continuum mass and momentum conservation. It introduces rotating frames, absolute circulation, layer potential vorticity, constant-depth reduction, spherical inversion, energy and enstrophy, damping, and finite-memory forcing. The assumptions of each reduction are stated separately.
The mathematical prerequisites are vector calculus, orthogonal expansions, and spectral numerical methods. The fluid chapters also define the operators and probability needed for their derivations.
These chapters share a source with the physical-prerequisites document. The book includes the parcel-kinematics and transport derivations, while cross-referencing its vector-calculus chapters for the shared operator theory. It retains the general fluid theory and excludes the companion’s implementation appendix. Equation labels prefixed P refer to the companion document’s stable chapter-equation numbers, independently of the book’s chapter ordering.
Primary sources are Vallis (2006), The Barotropic Vorticity Equation (n.d.), and Arfken and Weber (2005). The specific finite-memory stirring process comes from Vallis et al. (2004). The angular convention here is longitude \(\lambda\), latitude \(\phi\); other book chapters use colatitude \(\theta=\pi/2-\phi\) and longitude \(\varphi\). This is a change of coordinates, not a change in the harmonic normalization: \(\int |Y_\ell^m|^2d\omega=1\) in both.

title: 11  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
11.1 Fields, parcels, and the material derivative
Equations prefixed P retain the numbering of the companion physical-prerequisites document. Mathematical operators are introduced in vector calculus and integral theorems. Parcel derivatives and transport are developed in fluid kinematics.
Result and motivation. A derivative at a fixed location differs from the rate experienced by a moving fluid parcel by an advection term. This distinction turns Newton’s law into a field equation. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.1–1.2)
A continuum replaces molecular positions with smoothly varying averages on scales large compared with molecular spacing. Let \(\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)\) be Cartesian position, \(t\) time, and \(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)\) the velocity field, with units \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A parcel is a small collection of fluid that moves with the velocity. Its trajectory \(\mathbf{X}(t)\) satisfies \(d\mathbf{X}/dt=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{X}(t),t)\). The Eulerian description uses fields at fixed \(\mathbf{x}\); the Lagrangian description follows \(\mathbf{X}(t)\).
For a scalar field \(b(\mathbf{x},t)\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}b(\mathbf{X}(t),t)
=\frac{\partial b}{\partial t}
+\frac{dX_x}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial x}
+\frac{dX_y}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial y}
+\frac{dX_z}{dt}\frac{\partial b}{\partial z}.
\]
The material derivative, denoted \(D/Dt\), is therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac{Db}{Dt}=\partial_t b+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla b.}
\tag{P1.1}
\]
Here \(\partial_t\) means the partial derivative with respect to time; \(\nabla\) is the spatial gradient introduced in vector calculus. The term \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla b\) is advection, the change caused by transport through a spatial gradient. In Cartesian components, \(D\mathbf{v}/Dt=\partial_t\mathbf{v}+(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}\) is parcel acceleration. A steady field (\(\partial_t b=0\)) need not be materially constant (\(Db/Dt=0\)).
For example, take \(b=b_0+Gx\) and a uniform velocity \(\mathbf{v}=U\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). Here \(b_0\) is a constant, \(G\) a constant spatial gradient, \(U\) a speed, and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) the eastward Cartesian unit vector. Then \(\partial_t b=0\), but \(Db/Dt=UG\). This will matter when a parcel moves across latitude-dependent planetary vorticity.

title: 11  Kinematics and mathematical language
11  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
11.3 Material volumes and transport
Result and motivation. The integral of a field over a moving volume changes both because the field changes and because the volume expands. This is the bridge from parcel conservation to local balance laws. (Vallis 2006, sec. 1.2)
Let \(V(t)\) move with the fluid. An infinitesimal material volume \(\delta V\) changes at the rate \(D\delta V/Dt=(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v})\delta V\): differences between velocities on opposite faces give the three normal expansion rates in the divergence definition. Summing over the moving volume gives the transport theorem
 \[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V(t)}b\,dV
=\int_{V(t)}\left(\frac{Db}{Dt}+b\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}\right)dV
=\int_{V(t)}\left(\partial_tb+\nabla\cdot(b\mathbf{v})\right)dV.
\tag{P1.4}
\]
Here \(b\) is a density per unit volume of whatever is being integrated. It need not be mass density. For a material area \(A(t)\) transported by a tangent velocity \(\mathbf{u}\) on a surface, the analogous area change is \(D\delta A/Dt=(\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u})\delta A\). The subscript \(h\) denotes operators within the horizontal surface. Thus non-divergent surface motion preserves area.

title: 11  Kinematics and mathematical language
text:
11.4 Chapter summary

A field is an Eulerian quantity; a trajectory follows a Lagrangian parcel. Parcel acceleration is \(\partial_t\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{v}\).
The material derivative (P1.1) combines local change and advection.
Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian are defined in the vector-calculus chapter. Divergence and Stokes theorems connect local derivatives with flux and circulation.
The transport theorem (P1.4) includes material volume expansion. Non-divergent motion preserves the relevant volume or area.





Arfken, George B., and Hans J. Weber. 2005. Mathematical Methods for Physicists. 6th ed. Elsevier Academic Press.


Vallis, Geoffrey K. 2006. Atmospheric and Oceanic Fluid Dynamics: Fundamentals and Large-Scale Circulation. Cambridge University Press.

title: 12  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
12.1 Mass conservation and incompressibility
Equations prefixed P retain the numbering of the companion physical-prerequisites document. Mathematical operators are introduced in vector calculus and integral theorems. Parcel derivatives and transport are developed in fluid kinematics.
Result and motivation. Conservation of parcel mass gives the continuity equation. Incompressibility constrains volume change; it does not by itself make density spatially uniform. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.2, 1.9)
Let \(\rho(\mathbf{x},t)>0\) be mass density (\(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)). A material volume contains constant mass, so set \(b=\rho\) in (P1.4). Because this holds for every material volume,
\[
\boxed{\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{v})=0,
\qquad \frac{D\rho}{Dt}=-\rho\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}.}
\tag{P2.1}
\]
An incompressible flow preserves parcel volume: \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\). Then \(D\rho/Dt=0\), although different parcels can retain different densities. A homogeneous fluid has spatially uniform density. The constant-density, incompressible model uses one fixed density \(\rho_0\). These distinctions prevent the incorrect inference that incompressibility alone removes buoyancy (acceleration due to density contrasts in gravity) or density gradients.
Three-dimensional incompressibility gives \(\partial_xu+\partial_yv=-\partial_zw\), where \((u,v,w)\) are velocity components. Thus horizontal divergence need not vanish in an incompressible three-dimensional fluid. The later BVE imposes the stronger, separate restriction \(\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u}=0\) on the horizontal velocity \(\mathbf{u}=(u,v)\).

title: 12  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
12.2 Pressure, stress, and body forces
Result and motivation. Newton’s law balances parcel acceleration against pressure forces, viscous stress, and body forces. The constant-viscosity Laplacian is a special case of the stress divergence. (Vallis 2006, sec. 1.3)
Pressure \(p\) is the compressive normal force per unit area (\(\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\)). A surface with outward normal \(\mathbf{n}\) experiences traction \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf{n}\), where the stress tensor \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) maps a surface orientation to force per area. Write \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-p\mathbf{I}+\boldsymbol{\tau}\), where \(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity tensor and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) the viscous stress. Let \(\mathbf{b}\) be body force per unit mass (\(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)), such as gravity.
Newton’s law on a material volume is
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{V(t)}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV
=\int_{\partial V(t)}\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf{n}\,dA
+\int_{V(t)}\rho\mathbf{b}\,dV.
\]
Apply (P1.4), cancel terms using (P2.1), and apply the divergence theorem component by component to the stress. Localization gives
 \[
\boxed{\rho\frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt}=-\nabla p+\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}+\rho\mathbf{b}.}
\tag{P2.2}
\]
In Cartesian components, \((\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau})_i=\sum_j\partial_j\tau_{ij}\). The indices \(i,j\) run over three coordinate directions. Every term has units of force per volume. Pressure accelerates fluid toward lower pressure; a uniform pressure has no bulk acceleration because forces on opposite faces cancel.
For a constant-density, incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant dynamic viscosity \(\mu\geq0\) (\(\mathrm{Pa\,s}\)), the viscous force density is \(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}\). Newtonian means local viscous shear stress is proportional to local shear rate. This is a constitutive assumption about the material, not a consequence of Newton’s second law. We use the constant-density viscosity model of Vallis, sec. 1.3.3; a general compressible stress law requires additional terms. With \(\nu=\mu/\rho_0\) the kinematic viscosity (\(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\)), (P2.2) becomes the incompressible Navier-Stokes equation
 \[
\frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt}=-\frac{1}{\rho_0}\nabla p+\nu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{b},
\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0.
\tag{P2.3}
\]
Dropping viscous stress gives the Euler equation. A force is conservative if it is minus a potential gradient: \(\mathbf{b}=-\nabla\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) has units \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\). Its curl vanishes. This property, rather than the mere absence of friction, is needed for circulation conservation.

title: 12  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
12.3 Pressure closure and kinetic energy
Result and motivation. Incompressible pressure enforces the divergence constraint. Viscosity dissipates kinetic energy, whereas pressure redistributes it in a closed constant-density domain. (Vallis 2006, secs. 1.4, 1.10)
In the unrotating, constant-density system with conservative body force, define \(\Pi=p/\rho_0+\Phi\). Take the divergence of (P2.3). Since \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\) at all times,
\[
\nabla^2\Pi=-\nabla\cdot[(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v}].
\]
Thus pressure is determined diagnostically by an elliptic equation: a spatial boundary-value problem, here a Poisson equation, solved across the domain at each time, rather than independently stepped in time. An additive spatial constant in pressure does not affect motion. This closure is specific to the incompressible reduction. A compressible atmosphere instead also needs an equation of state and a thermodynamic evolution law. For example \(p=\rho R T\) relates ideal-gas pressure, absolute temperature \(T\), and specific gas constant \(R\); it is not by itself a complete evolution system. The constant-density BVE does not retain that thermodynamic system.
Let \(K=|\mathbf{v}|^2/2\) be kinetic energy per unit mass (\(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\)). Dot (P2.3) with \(\mathbf{v}\). Use \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\Pi=\nabla\cdot(\Pi\mathbf{v})\) and \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{v}=\nabla^2K-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jv_i)^2\). On a periodic volume,
 \[
\frac{d}{dt}\int_V K\,dV
=-\nu\int_V\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jv_i)^2\,dV\leq0.
\tag{P2.4}
\]
Flux terms integrate to zero by periodicity. The same conclusion holds with suitable stationary no-slip walls. Locally, pressure can do work; its net contribution vanishes under these boundary conditions. Molecular viscosity removes kinetic energy into internal energy; neglecting heat in the reduced equations does not change the sign of this kinetic-energy sink.

title: 12  Mass, forces, and the momentum equation
text:
12.4 Chapter summary

Density \(\rho\), pressure \(p\), stress \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\), and body acceleration \(\mathbf{b}\) enter mass conservation (P2.1) and momentum conservation (P2.2).
Incompressibility means volume preservation; homogeneity means spatially uniform density. Horizontal non-divergence is an additional restriction.
The viscous term \(\nu\nabla^2\mathbf{v}\) requires constant viscosity and incompressibility. The inviscid counterpart is Euler’s equation.
Incompressible pressure enforces the velocity constraint. Conservative forces are potential gradients. Viscosity is a kinetic-energy sink under the stated boundary conditions.
